newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude ends modestly higher on technicals.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude ends modestly higher on technicals.

text.p: NYMEX crude prices ended modestly higher Monday, paring larger gains made early session on technical strength and news ethnic clashes in Nigeria continued to disrupt oil production there.
June crude ended up three cents at $19.63 a barrel after rising as high as $19.88 before late profit-taking set in. The closure of London's IPE due to a U.K. holiday thinned trade.

"Today was a wash. At the end, local players picked each others' pockets, and we ended near unchanged which is better since we can have a real day tomorrow when London is open," said a New York crude dealer.

On the charts, June crude bounced early session from trendline support that extends from the low of April 10 on the daily spot continuation chart through the session low April 17. Refined products also had bounced from trendline support, giving the oil complex a technical strength that lasted until the close, traders said.
June heating oil settled up 0.03 cent a gallon at 53.05 cents a gallon, and June gasoline ended up 0.02 cent a gallon at 60.54 cents.
There was scant news for fundamental players, but little that there was propped oil prices.

Nigeria's semi-official newspaper the Daily Times on Saturday quoted Nigeria's oil minister Dan Etete as saying a 125,000 barrel per day (bpd) oil refinery in the midwestern city of Warri had been shut following recent ethnic clashes.
Etete said a fuel shortage could hit western Nigeria if the facility was not reopened soon.

Meanwhile, Royal Dutch Shell Group's Nigerian unit said it reopened four of five of its flow stations after being shut due to the ethnic clashes. Royal Dutch Shell's 2,000 bpd Warri flow station remained closed.

Still, dealers noted some clearinghouses are known to start their crude expiry role around the fifth of the month, so front month crude could start to weaken as June is sold and July is bought. The June crude contract expires May 20.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
